On April 23, Barcelona, by then managed by Tito Vilanova, were hammered 4-0 by Bayern Munich-the side Pep Guardiola, who had quit to take a sabbatical in New York, was set to take over when Jupp Heynckes's contract expired the following summer. The next night, Jürgen Klopp's Borussia Dortmund savaged Real Madrid, beating them 4-1. In both cases, the German side had less possession. But they weren't clinging on, holding out against the siege, and stealing something on the break: in both cases, the German side looked quicker, stronger, and sharper. This was a systematic approach based on counterattacking, and it had finalized the process begun by Internazionale in 2010 and Chelsea in 2012: it ended the obsession with ball retention.

There were predictable snide comments-the age of social media, after all, was fully upon the world-about Bayern's folly in appointing as their new manager the high priest of a style their outgoing manager had just exposed, but that was to miss the point. It was reasonable to feel sympathy for Heynckes, who would end up being ousted having won a treble, but the new German style was less an antidote to the Spanish game than a variant of it. What clouded the issue was the focus on possession. Barcelona at their best, like Ajax before them, had excelled not merely at keeping the ball but at winning it back. Guardiola's Barça were probably the greatest side at holding onto the ball there has ever been, but they also excelled at pressing, and it was that aspect that the new German style prioritized.

<!-- image -->

Germany's attitude towards pressing was always a little perplexing. Bayern and Borussia Mönchengladbach in the seventies played a possession game, but it was never predicated on pressing. Rather, West German soccer retained a man-marking structure in which the *libero* became the effective playmaker as the other nine players on the field dealt with their direct opponent.

The Austrian Ernst Happel did introduce zonal marking during his stint with Hamburg, but he never had them press as hard as he had, for instance, the Feyenoord team with which he won the European Cup in 1970. In the Netherlands, he had been a pioneer of pressing, almost as though he and Rinus Michels, who was at Ajax at the time, drove each other to greater and greater heights. The similarity in approach was sufficient for Happel to seem the obvious choice to lead Holland at the 1978 World Cup. Happel used the style with some success at Club Brugge as well, taking them to a European Cup final in which they were beaten by Liverpool, but by the time he became the first manager to win the European Cup with two different sides (with Hamburg in 1983), he had tempered his approach. A difficult spell with Sevilla in 1973-1974, perhaps, had taught him that the same approach doesn't necessarily work everywhere; West Germany in the early eighties simply might not have been ready for pressing.

As the decade went on, 5-3-2 became a viable alternative to 4-3-3, but zonal marking was still generally regarded as needless foreign over-complication. Games were to be won by character and by the efforts of the *Führungsspieler* -the Franz Beckenbauer or Lothar Matthäus figure who could inspire his men to glory. And for a long time, it worked: between 1972 and 1996, (West) Germany won two World Cups and three European Championships, while losing in three major finals.

But there were doubters, foremost among them Ralf Rangnick. Born in 1958, the defensive midfielder began his career at VfB Stuttgart but never made it beyond their amateur side. He studied English and sports science at the University of Stuttgart, a course that included a year at the University of Sussex, where he became a devout Anglophile. One of his classmates in Stuttgart played professional volleyball for Feuerbach, and he was struck by how much training she did: ten hours a day, including gym work and two hours purely on tactics. He came to wonder whether soccer was stuck in its ways, a little backwards in that regard.

Rangnick drifted through Germany's lower leagues before, at the age of twenty-four, becoming player-manager of the sixth-tier side Viktoria Backnang. In February 1983, they played a friendly against Valeriy Lobanovskyi's Dynamo Kyiv, who were staying at Sportschule Ruit for a winter training camp. It was, he later said, "an epiphany." When the ball went out of play for a throw-in early on, Rangnick counted the Dynamo players, half believing they'd sneaked an extra man onto the field. They hadn't; but such was the ferocity of their pressing that it felt like they had. Rangnick had never experienced anything like it before. Dynamo kept coming to Ruit and Rangnick kept studying them.

In 1985, Rangnick became coach of VfB Stuttgart's amateur side. At around the same time, he met Helmut Groß, a structural engineer who had essentially taught himself tactical theory and was part of a think tank trying to pass ideas on to younger coaches. While manager of the sixth-flight side SC Geislingen, he had observed how efficient zonal marking was in terms of energy conservation. That excess energy, he reasoned, could be employed to press higher up the field. Groß had no soccer background, which meant he was treated with a certain skepticism, but he was far from a crank. With the fifth-division side Kirchheim, he twice won the Baden-Württemberg championship and once even held Dynamo to a 1-1 draw. In 1984, his successor at Geislingen, Jakob Baumann, led his side to a shock 2-0 victory over Happel's Hamburg SV in the DFB Cup.

Groß and Rangnick became good friends, sitting up late into the night to discuss tactics and watch videos they had shipped from Italy of Arrigo Sacchi's Milan. In 1989, Groß was put in charge of VfB Stuttgart's youth setup and made pressing mandatory for all development sides. Rangnick, who had been convinced that players of any level could prosper by pressing after implementing the system at SC Korb in the German seventh flight, soon followed him to the club, after being appointed reserve-team coach.

Slowly zonal marking and pressing began to spread throughout Germany. Volker Finke, another coach who had had no professional playing career to speak of, took charge of Freiburg in 1991. He led them to promotion to the Bundesliga in 1993. They narrowly avoided relegation the following season but made their mark with a number of emphatic wins against top sides: 3-1 over Bayern, 4-1 over Dortmund, 4-0 at Stuttgart. The following season was even better, as they hammered Bayern 5-1 on the second weekend and went on to finish third. Yet Finke still wasn't taken entirely seriously and, when economic reality hit and Freiburg began to slide, it seemed to confirm the wisdom of the conservative establishment.

Gradually, though, a revolution was brewing. Wolfgang Frank had been a Bundesliga striker for Eintracht Braunschweig in the seventies, but his biggest influence was Sacchi. When he was appointed coach of Mainz in the second division in September 1995, they had one point and no goals from eight games. He explained his ideas and set about implementing them, benefiting from taking over a side that essentially had nothing left to lose. It was hard, boring work: learning positioning, walking around in prearranged patterns on the training field. "But," said the team's center-back, Jürgen Klopp, "we thought if Gullit and Van Basten had to learn that at Milan, we could put up with it as well." They stayed up and the next season finished fourth.

Rangnick, meanwhile, went to Reutlingen and then Ulm, whom he led to promotion to the second flight in 1997-1998. That summer, Germany were embarrassed at the World Cup, playing grim, functional soccer before being outplayed by Ćiro Blažević's Croatia in the quarterfinal. Success at Euro 96 (with a drab, clanking squad), it quickly became accepted, had been something of a freak. But just because there were doubts over the old ways didn't mean there was any consensus on which way German soccer should turn.

The following season, Ulm began with sixteen games unbeaten. In December 1998, Rangnick was invited on *ZDF Sportstudio* , a Bundesliga highlights show, to discuss zonal marking and a flat back-four which, if the tone of the presenter is anything to go by, seemed to be regarded by the wider soccer public less as basic tactical concepts and more as kabbalistic mumbo jumbo. In ninety cogent seconds, the slim and bespectacled Rangnick explained his system, pointing out that the focus on a *libero* , a free man, made little sense in a world that had largely abandoned man-marking. Germany, though, perhaps still wasn't ready to hear the message. There was a backlash from the establishment, and Rangnick was derided as "a professor" and "a theorist."

Subsequent events gave his critics ammunition. Rangnick left Ulm for Stuttgart in March 1999. Ulm went on to win promotion, but Rang-nick faltered at the bigger club. That he was their fifth manager in a year perhaps should have been a warning. More practically, the transition to Rangnick's approach was always going to be difficult for a side used to playing through a playmaker in the fan-favorite Krassimir Balakov. Rang-nick's relationship with the Bulgarian was never easy, but it collapsed completely when Balakov swore at him after being substituted in a league game against 1860 Munich. Balakov was suspended but, with results disappointing, Rangnick was soon sacked. Could his methods, it was asked, really work with higher-profile players who might not be prepared to subjugate their egos to the needs of the team?

Yet while there were doubts about Rangnick, there were even bigger doubts about the way German soccer as a whole was going. The 1998 World Cup had been a wake-up call. Berti Vogts was hounded out of his job the following September and replaced by Erich Ribbeck. At sixty-one, he was not a man likely to lead a revolution. Far more significant, it turned out, were reforms the DFB had begun to introduce to youth coaching. Alarmed that a lack of players, forwards in particular, had led to the South African Sean Dundee and the Brazilian Paulo Rink being naturalized to cover a dearth of German strikers, the DFB appointed the former Kaiserslautern, Eintracht Frankfurt, Fortuna Düsseldorf, and Egypt coach Dietrich Weise to oversee the establishment of 121 regional centers across Germany. Euro 2000, in which Germany were eliminated in the group stage, even losing to Kevin Keegan's England, confirmed just how bad things had become. Germany played what became derided as *Rumpelfußball* : the team was old, they lumbered around, and in 2001 they lost a World Cup qualifier 5-1 at home to England.

But this was a very German crisis. Bayern still won the Champions League in 2001 and, making the most of a fortunate draw, Germany, by then managed by Rudi Völler, reached the final of the World Cup in 2002. They were still, by and large, disciplined; still tough enough to win tight games; and, in Oliver Kahn, had a highly gifted goalkeeper who fit the ethos of the team perfectly. By 2002, Germany had become about "Kahn, *Kampf und Kopfball* "-Kahn, struggle, and heading-a pastiche of the *Turniermannschaft* -tournament side-identity of which they'd once been so proud.

It was then that the wisdom of the post-1998 review really began to be seen. Graduates of Weise's development centers started to come through. The clubs were cajoled into establishing their own academies. Changes in 2001 made it easier for immigrants and their children to secure German citizenship, making it possible for thousands of potential players to play for Germany who would otherwise have been lost-as Yıldıray Baştürk, Ümit Davala, and İlhan Mansız, all of whom were born in Germany but played for Turkey, had been.

The revolution wasn't only bottom-up but also top-down, as Jürgen Klinsmann was appointed manager of the national side, assisted by Jogi Löw, who had worked with Groß at Stuttgart. Klinsmann's insistence on living in California and his habit of speaking business jargon inflected with vague New Age pretension didn't endear him to everybody, but his time playing in Italy, France, and England had opened his eyes to other ways of approaching the game. He introduced systematic pressing, got the players fitter, and made them work in a far more structured way on transitions. He also dropped Kahn for Jens Lehmann-a mobile goalkeeper more in step with the post-Cruyffian demand that the goalkeeper should be able to operate at times as a quasi-outfielder-and in so doing enacted a radical change in the template of the German goalkeeper, leading ultimately to Manuel Neuer, the ultimate sweeper-keeper.

Quite how adept Klinsmann was as a manager is debatable-subsequent spells with Bayern and the United States didn't work out well-and there is a sense that Germany's success at the 2006 World Cup, when they finished third having played much brighter, slicker soccer than they had in years, was the result as much of the generally euphoric home atmosphere as of anything the coaching staff did. What is clear is that he opened the door to a new era in German soccer, one on which Löw capitalized. He replaced Klinsmann after the World Cup and, after defeats in the final of Euro 2008 and the semifinals of the 2010 World Cup and Euro 2012, lifted the World Cup in 2014, by which time twenty-one of the twenty-three-man squad had come through the academy system. The speed of the national side had increased significantly: in 2005, an average of 2.8 seconds passed between a player controlling and passing the ball; by 2010, that gap was less than a second.

The confirmation that the new ways of press-and-possess had been fully adopted came in 2005 when Klopp, who had replaced Frank as manager of Mainz and, after two near misses, had in 2004 led them to promotion to the Bundesliga for the first time, was invited by ZDF to be a studio pundit for their coverage of the Confederations Cup. He designed a video tool to help explain tactical issues and, in the same studio where Rangnick had alienated the establishment seven years earlier, became a huge success. Perhaps Rangnick was simply preaching his message too soon, or perhaps Klopp's charisma and his self-deprecating wit made it easier for the audience to relate to him, but what was clear was that the national mood had changed. Soccer was no longer merely about personalities and leadership; tactical discussion, which by then meant zonal marking and pressing, had entered the German mainstream.

Rangnick led Schalke 04 to second in the league in 2004-2005 and then achieved astonishing success with Hoffenheim, where he employed Groß as his advisor and the former national hockey coach Bernhard Peters as his assistant. Two promotions took the village club to the Bundesliga and, in 2017, under another young coach who favored a pressing game, Julian Nagelsmann, they qualified for the Champions League play-offs for the first time. Returning to Schalke, Rangnick got them to a Champions League semifinal, but it was Klopp who became the face of the new style.

Mainz were relegated in 2007 and, having failed to gain promotion the following season, Klopp resigned. He was appointed at Borussia Dortmund, who had just finished thirteenth, and he led them to sixth and then fifth, before winning the title in both 2011 and 2012. His style, *Gegenpressing* , began to draw attention from across Europe. *Gegenpressing* , Klopp said, "is the best playmaker in the world." Win the ball back quickly, high up the field, when the opposition is disoriented, and the chances almost created themselves.

But it wasn't kick-and-rush. It wasn't just about tempo and energy. "When three players chase in a swarm after a ball that's just been lost, it can sometimes look chaotic," Groß said. "But this is chaos of a controlled and highly creative kind." Klopp had learned from Frank and so in that sense was influenced by Sacchi. Having been born in Stuttgart, he is often seen as part of a Swabian school with Rangnick and Löw, and he is open in his admiration of Lobanovskyi. In his desire to win the ball back quickly high up the field, Klopp is like Bielsa or Guardiola. Klopp himself has never made any secret of his love for English soccer and the way it dominated Europe in the late seventies and early eighties with a form of pressing game. When Klopp was appointed Liverpool manager in 2015, there was a strange sense that he was selling back to its creator, in slightly modernized, more sophisticated form, the English game of thirty years earlier-before the Heysel ban and the loss of confidence, before the vain scrabble through the Dutch, French, Spanish, and German games for some imagined secret formula that could reinvigorate English soccer.

Klopp's success at Dortmund confirmed the new style could be effective at the highest level. As a new generation of coaches-the likes of Roger Schmidt, Thomas Tuchel, and Tayfun Korkut-began to be appointed to Bundesliga jobs, *Gegenpressing* began to diversify. Klopp's sides would essentially encircle the man in possession, giving him no space to play a pass. When Heynckes adopted *Gegenpressing* in 2012-2013, the season Bayern won the double, he preferred a man-oriented variant. One player would go to the opponent with the ball, while others would seek to mark possible recipients of a pass, cutting down the options of the man in possession. Nagelsmann's sides tended to focus on the passing lanes, looking to insert themselves between the man on the ball and potential recipients of a pass, relying more on interceptions than on making tackles. That perhaps required more thought from the players, but it meant that when possession was regained, the man winning the ball should have more time and space to initiate an attack.

**Klopp's Dortmund (DFB-Pokal final, 2012)**

image

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

I t wasn't just Germany where *Gegenpressing* took hold. This, though, was a new style of tactical revolution. Neoliberal economics had changed soccer utterly. Where previously a great club had risen with a group of great players playing the perfect soccer for that group of players, only to fall away as their secrets were understood, age sapped their zip, success drained their hunger, and the emotional attrition of constant exposure to one another eroded the bonds of team spirit, by 2013 soccer had entered the era of the super-clubs. The elite by then were so much richer than the rest, the financial structures of soccer so rigged to perpetuate the flow of wealth, that it became impossible for the biggest clubs to fall any great distance. In the season in which they lost 7-0 over two legs to Bayern and the style they had made their own ceased to be dominant, Barça won the league.

Illness forced Tito Vilanova to quit that summer. His replacement, Gerardo Martino, had been a key part of Bielsa's Newell's side in the early nineties and had made significant progress using a cautious interpretation of his pressing style with Paraguay, leading them to the final of the 2011 Copa América. He never really settled, though, and was gone within a year, replaced by Luis Enrique. Persuading the midfielder to leave Real Madrid for the Camp Nou had been just about Johan Cruyff's last act as manager of Barcelona, and Luis Enrique became a teammate of Guardiola during the extraordinary period when Louis van Gaal was manager and Ronald Koeman and José Mourinho were his assistants. From a tactical point of view, modern soccer was forged during that period at Barcelona.

Luis Enrique ended his first season in charge by winning a treble, yet in January 2015, he had seemed on his way out, with Barça apparently mired in crisis. That, perhaps, is also a feature of the age of the super-club: success becomes so expected that the slightest dip in form or results prompts panic, and long-term thinking becomes all but impossible-something that makes tactical radicalism far less likely.

Barça had signed Neymar for a basic fee of around £50 million in 2013 and Luis Suárez for £65 million a year later, deals that seemed simultaneously to excite and unsettle fans. The players' quality was not in doubt, but equally the signings seemed to signal a move towards a *galáctico* model similar to that employed by Real Madrid, and thus away from the team ethic and the reliance on the *cantera* that represented Barça's self-image. It's hard to claim to be *més que un club* when you're just signing celebrities like everybody else.

When the season began disappointingly, that unease became anger. Luis Enrique had declared "hunting season" open in November 2014 after Barcelona's first ever home defeat to Celta Vigo. When they lost 1-0 at home to Real Sociedad in the first game back after the winter break, his future seemed very uncertain indeed, particularly given that he had left Messi out of that game. Messi had been on the bench for his first game back after spending Christmas in Argentina in both of the two previous seasons, but this time it was perceived as evidence of a rift between player and coach. Rumors of a breakdown in their relationship were only fueled when Messi then skipped a training session, blaming gastroenteritis, which Xavi had unhelpfully revealed the previous week was the excuse usually given when a player has other reasons not to train. The defender Jérémy Mathieu admitted Messi and Luis Enrique had clashed.

Off the field, Barcelona's image had been sullied by a transfer ban imposed because of irregularities in how they'd signed Under-16s and by ongoing allegations over the signing of Neymar. The club legend Andoni Zubizarreta was dismissed as director of soccer and his assistant, Carles Puyol, the former captain, soon followed. Luis Enrique admitted his position had been "weakened," ' and a poll suggested 68 percent of fans wanted him gone.

But then Barça scraped a win over Atlético that suggested some fight remained in the side. Messi returned to the middle and a false nine role, with Luis Suárez shifting to the right. That brought greater fluidity, and Barça won thirty-one of their final thirty-five games of the season, including a 3-1 victory over Juventus in the Champions League final. Yet was it Luis Enrique's doing? Suárez let slip that the switch that got the front three performing so well was something that happened almost organically during a game, when the Argentinian eventually told him to stay where he was after he had drifted into the middle.

But to suggest Luis Enrique was nothing more than a figurehead-somebody who is wise enough to know when to shut up and let the players get on with it, although that is in itself a skill-would be misleading. His management of Xavi's decline could hardly have gone better, although he found Xavi a far more biddable soul that he himself had been as Frank Rijkaard eased him out of the side in 2003-2004. And, most significantly, he oversaw the transition to a more varied style, which was perhaps not surprising: after all, he was not as steeped in Barça's traditions as Guardiola was; he came through not at la Masía but at Sporting de Gijón's academy.

Six of the Barça side that played against Juventus in Berlin in that 2015 final had also played against Manchester United in Rome in 2009. In one sense, that represents a remarkable level of continuity; only four players who played for Real Madrid in the 1956 European Cup final-Marquitos, José María Zárraga, Francisco Gento, and Alfredo di Stéfano-also played when they won it for a fifth time in a row in 1960. Continuity, though, will take you only so far. After Guardiola's departure, there had been a sense of drift. Perhaps Barça had lost their desire; perhaps Vilanova and Martino simply hadn't been able to inspire them. Certainly they looked fitter under Luis Enrique. But there was also a feeling that they had become too harmonious, that their constant passing, their reluctance to play the risky ball or attempt the dribble that might lose possession, made them at times predictable. A devout Cruyffian might even have suggested that they had become too much like a Van Gaal side. Inter and Chelsea may have ridden their luck to beat them in the Champions League semifinals in 2010 and 2012, but they had shown the way: after those games everybody knew that the best chance of beating Barça was to sit back and deny them space and the possibility of verticality, making them pass the ball horizontally across the field. Where teams would once have been terrified by the prospect of having only 20 percent possession in a game, that became accepted as the most effective way against such a radical possession side.

That's why the signings of Neymar and Suárez were so significant. Their individual ability meant they could disrupt marking structures by beating a couple of men with a dribble, making it far harder for opponents simply to sit deep against Barça. Messi, of course, had always offered that element of chaos, but three soloists are far harder to defend against than one: the statistics showed that Barça dribbled three times more frequently in 2014-2015 than they had in 2010-2011. Ivan Rakitić, similarly, offered a new aspect in midfield: quicker, riskier, and more direct forward passes-looking to release that front three, rather than being a sophisticated lubricant in the way Xavi had been. Perhaps the Barça of 2015 was not as pure as that of 2011, they were not a distillation of post-Cruyffianism, but those impurities made them harder to stop.

But there was a cost. Two years later, Barça, having survived a remarkable last-sixteen tie in the Champions League against Paris Saint-Germain-in which they lost 4-0 in the first leg-were well beaten by Juventus in the quarterfinal. As they finished second behind Real Madrid in the league, a mood of general dissatisfaction hung over the club. The remnants of Guardiola's great side were aging, new signings hadn't worked out, the production line from la Masía had slowed, and Neymar, who had been lined up as Messi's successor, left for PSG. Worse, the sense of Barcelona as something unique, as the manifestation of a philosophy, had gone. They were just another wealthy club, struggling to cope with the transfer market. Wealth insulated them and there was no dramatic decline, but the specialness had gone. Perhaps that was inevitable-no academy can simply produce great players to order-but it didn't dull the pain. The appointment of Ernesto Valverde, who had played under Cruyff at Barça in the late eighties, felt like a conscious attempt to drag the club back to its principles, although the result was an oddly insipid 4-4-2 that was good enough to win la Liga but the defensive inadequacies of which were exposed by Chelsea in the Champions League even before the surrender of a 4-1 first-leg lead in the Champions League quarterfinal against Roma.

**Luis Enrique's Barcelona (Champions League final, 2015)**

image

<!-- image -->

Those Champions League defeats to PSG and Juventus were the continuation of the process begun in the 2013 Champions League semifinals. Barça, in part sustained by the finances of modern soccer, had not gone away. They had not collapsed or sunk into the sort of decline suffered by Inter after their defeat to Celtic in 1967 or by Ajax after the departure of Cruyff. They were still there at the top table, habitual challengers in the Champions League, just about able to conceive of finishing third in la Liga, but certainly no lower. Their style, though, whether referred to as tiki-taka, a term Guardiola abhors, or *juego de posición* , is no longer hegemonic. Spain, too, suffered their defeats, savaged 5-1 by a series of counterattacks at the 2014 World Cup as Louis van Gaal's Holland played against type. They were then harried and pressed to a 2-0 defeat by Jorge Sampaoli's Chile and eliminated. At Euro 2016, after an unconvincing group stage, sluggish going forward and unable to deal with their rapid transitions, Spain were undone by Antonio Conte's Italy.

All three key defeats came against sides playing a back three. "When Italy need to come out with the ball, having three at the back and two wide players means they have five possible people to carry it out-which makes it difficult for Spain to press as they would like," Xavi had explained in *La Gazzetta dello Sport* before the meeting in Paris. "Then, playing with two strikers complicates things further forward, because it occupies both of our centre-backs and then one of the two full-backs has to step forward to close down [Antonio] Candreva or [Alessandro] Florenzi-leaving you with only three at the back. At the World Cup in Brazil, both Holland and Chile chose to use a 3-5-2 against us and it put us in great difficulty."

Shape, assuredly, was part of it-and getting the extra man into mid-field, getting the full-backs higher up the field as wing-backs, was a major reason why the back three began to return to fashion. But there was also a sense of Spain following Barça-understandably, given how many of the players were the same-in becoming a little stale and so unable to deal with the ferocity of opponents who, smelling blood, pressed against them. It's perhaps not so much that the style of 2011 has been superseded as that the second final against United was an apotheosis: a core of players who had grown up together playing a radical style that was perfect for them.

<!-- image -->

F or teams who wanted to press high up the field, or even teams who wanted to counter that pressing, the back three had begun to make a comeback. Gian Piero Gasperini, for instance, had begun to use a back three in that way during his time at Genoa and took Atalanta to a fourth-place finish in Serie A in 2016-2017, overwhelming teams by pressing with five midfielders.

The most striking use of a back three that season, though, was at Chelsea. Spooked into a change of formation having gone 3-0 down at Arsenal in their sixth game of the season, their manager Antonio Conte switched to a 3-4-2-1 at half-time and, although they lost that game, they won their next thirteen in the league and went on to win the title, becoming the first side to do so in England while fielding a back three since Everton in 1962-1963. Harry Catterick's side featured Brian Labone at center-half flanked at the back by Mick Meagan and either Alex Parker or George Thomson, the last hurrah in England of the W-M. The following year, Bill Shankly's Liverpool, operating a back four, won the league, and it was his thinking and that of Don Revie and Alf Ramsey that would dominate for half a century.

The immediate impact of the switch to a back four was to neuter the winger, but there was a corollary to that, which was the release of the full-back. Nílton Santos and Silvio Marzolini pioneered the idea of attacking from deep-lying wide areas and that strategy, uneasily and unevenly, spread. When England, belatedly, adopted the notion of a formation with three central defenders at the 1990 World Cup, they still clung to the notion that a full-back, as the name suggested (not that that had bothered them with center-halves), should be a defender. Their interpretation of a 5-3-2 featured not midfielders in the wide positions but Paul Parker and Stuart Pearce as full-backs who could get forward. But Brazil's use of Leandro and Júnior at the 1982 World Cup, to take just one example, had shown another way. In other cultures, the *lateral* was simply a player who operated wide; there was no preconception he should be first and foremost a defender.

**Conte's Chelsea (2016-17)**

image

<!-- image -->

By the late nineties, the back three was retreating in the face of single-striker systems. Once the full-back had tasted freedom, though, there was no turning him back. The advent of 4-2-3-1 and return to popularity of 4-3-3 pushed wide creators higher up the field, but full-backs remained an attacking presence.

That has become increasingly the case with the growing trend for inverted wingers. If a left-footed forward plays on the right, his effectiveness is significantly enhanced if he has a full-back overlapping outside him, presenting the full-back with the dilemma of defending on the inside-anticipating the forward coming onto his stronger, left, foot-or remaining in a neutral position in case the ball is pushed right to a full-back coming on the outside.

Conte took that further. There were times during the Euro 2016, notably against Spain in the last sixteen, when the Italy wing-backs, Mattia De Sciglio and Alessandro Florenzi, were pushed so high that the shape was almost 3-3-4 rather than 3-5-2. Guardiola, in his first season at Manchester City, at times deployed a back three, with Raheem Sterling and Leroy Sané or Nolito as his wide men, in what was effectively a 3-2-4-1. He took the idea that full-backs were to be regarded as midfielders more than defenders further than anybody. At Bayern, he would have David Alaba and Philipp Lahm tuck in to operate as central midfielders, forming the same trapezium with the back three that had been there in the defensive M of the W-M. He perhaps didn't have the personnel for that in his first season at City, but by the second he had Kyle Walker and Benjamin Mendy or Fabian Delph working the whole flank and often coming inside their winger, changing the angle of attack and exploiting the join between the opposing full-backs and central defenders.

But in 2016-2017, it was Conte, using a back three, who had the greatest success. For him, a back three was paradoxically more defensive than a back four, the insertion of David Luiz between César Azpilicueta and Gary Cahill offering protection that allowed Victor Moses and Marcos Alonso, the wing-backs, to act as midfielders. Their provision of attacking width in turn had an impact higher up the field. N'Golo Kanté and Nemanja Matić provided an extra layer of protection in front of the back four, that familiar trapezoid shape. With that platform in place, there was then freedom for Eden Hazard and Pedro (or Willian), operating essentially as inside-forwards behind a lone striker. Playing in that awkward niche between the opposing holding midfielders and the full-backs, unopposed as they once would have been by wing-halves, they frequently found themselves in pockets of space.

Chelsea weren't the first to use the shape: Brendan Rodgers had done so at Liverpool two seasons earlier (having been impressed by Paulo Sousa's use of it with Basel), and it could even be argued Roy Evans's Liverpool had played a similar shape in the midnineties. But Conte's side were the first to combine that shape with a ferocious pressing game, and in some ways they were the most successful. As opponents sought to work out a way of dealing with them, no fewer than thirteen of the twenty Premier League sides used some variant of a back three at various points in the season. That, perhaps, was simple geometric sense: playing that M shape at the back, using the trapezoid block as the basic defensive unit, does offer two holding midfielders who can operate as wing-halves once did, and so at least occupy the space sought by the inside-forwards.

Conte's other great strength is his work on positioning, which he practices using the shadow-play popularized by Arrigo Sacchi, but which was seemingly developed by Alan Brown at Sunderland in the early sixties. There again the influence of Lobanovskyi is felt, with Conte so concerned to keep the preprogrammed moves of his side secret that while Italy coach he forbade all but the closest members of his coaching staff to watch practice. "We work a lot of tactical positions and we know exactly what we have to do on the pitch, where I have to go and where the defenders have to go," the Chelsea winger Eden Hazard said, explaining the major differences between Conte and his predecessor at Stamford Bridge, José Mourinho. "We know exactly what to do. With Mourinho, he put in a system but we didn't work lots. We know what to do because we play football, but maybe the automatisms were a little bit different.... It's not always nice as a forward as you have to run, defend and everything, but at least at the weekend, you know exactly what to do, you can even close your eyes and play."

<!-- image -->

C onte's success was significant in that it brought together two of the biggest trends in soccer over the past couple of decades: the liberation of the full-back and the insistence on pressing. What marked him out as modern, though-or, at least, if Hazard is to be believed, more modern than Mourinho-was his work on coordinated attacking moves. In itself, of course, that is nothing new-managers as diverse as Herbert Chapman and Valeriy Lobanovskyi implemented clear structures of attacking play-and nor should such an approach be seen as prescriptive. Rather it is a theme on which great artists can extemporize, designed though familiarity to speed up attacking play by making complex moves semiautomatic. (This is also one of the reasons international soccer so often seems wanting in the modern age; national managers simply don't have the time with their players to generate the sort of mutual understanding from which true fluency derives.)

Hazard wasn't the only one to find Mourinho wanting in that regard: the most consistent criticism of him at Real Madrid, from a tactical point of view, was that he left the forwards to improvise rather than drilling them in how to break down the massed defenses they regularly came up against. Guardiola, similarly, in his obsession with *juego de posición* , is a manager who likes his sides to attack in preset ways.

But that's a detail, a preference-an evolution, perhaps, and something that will presumably only become more sophisticated as data analysis and computer modeling improves, but nothing as revolutionary as what Guardiola achieved with Barcelona. In the years since 2013 and the recognition that that style of radical possession was no longer hegemonic, what has followed is, broadly speaking, a multiplicity of Barça-inflected approaches.

There are exceptions, of course. Mourinho, since Guardiola got the Barcelona job ahead of him in 2008, seems almost willfully to be playing an anti-Barça style of soccer, using the lessons he learned working under Louis van Gaal in the late nineties to undermine the philosophy, almost reveling in winning games with minimal possession. The side he began the season with at Manchester United in 2017-2018 was the tallest in any of the top five leagues in Europe, demonstrating a preference for physical power over technique. The way his side bullied Peter Bosz's post-Cruyffian Ajax in the 2017 Europa League final was a prime example of how effective that way of playing can be.

Or there's Diego Simeone, brought up in an entirely different tradition: his first youth coach when he joined Veléz Sarsfield was Victorio Spinetto, and he has clearly absorbed many of his principles about the need for *fibra* . To say he practices *anti-fútbol* in the way it has been interpreted since Osvaldo Zubeldía's Estudiantes would be unfair, but equally he seizes whatever advantage he can, even if that means instructing ball-boys to throw additional balls onto the field to stop opposing attacks. At the same time, though, he has clearly been conditioned by his time playing at Atlético and in Italy.

This blurring of influences, perhaps, is the most notable feature of the modern game: managers and players move far more than ever before, constantly testing their ideas in new environments. What worked for Guardiola at Barça, for instance, had to be amended when he went to Bayern, and there was need of an even more significant rethink after he took the Manchester City job.

And then there's money, or rather its distribution. Elite soccer is dominated now as it never has been before by a handful of super-clubs. For many of them, winning their domestic title has come to be regarded almost as a formality. There are vast imbalances within leagues, and that, of course, conditions the tactical approach teams take. If you expect to win most games comfortably, everything becomes focused on attacking, which can cause problems for the super-clubs on the rare occasions they come up against team at around their level: they forget not merely how to defend but also how to fight. The standard of defending has declined alarmingly among elite clubs, something that's not just to do with a shift to a more attacking focus. In the eight seasons from 2009 to 2010, 21 of 104 games in the quarterfinals or later finished with a winning margin of three or more; in the eight seasons before that, there were only eight. In 2017-2018, there were even more: Liverpool against City, Real Madrid against Juventus, Barcelona against Roma, then Roma against Barcelona, and Liverpool against Roma. Never has a three-goal lead seemed less secure.

The need to generate revenue, meanwhile, has led to an increasing focus on the individual. Perhaps that's a natural consequence of an era that has enjoyed two players as ludicrously gifted as Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, but it also feels that the nature of the game has changed, that the soap opera culture that funds modern soccer requires stars and celebrities. Guardiola, at Barcelona at least, when he had an academy that produced players already inculcated with his style, stood in opposition to that; he has found it harder to succeed without spending since. The attitude of players, in turn, seems to have changed. It's hard to quantify, of course, but when Paul Pogba, on joining Manchester United in 2016, spoke less of hoping to win the league or the Champions League than of striving for the Ballon d'Or, it felt like a key moment. Players now ask at least as much what a club can do for them as what they can do for the club-and that means their willingness to submit themselves to a tactical system can be limited. That, allied with the constant pressure for results, inhibits experimentation and leads to tactical conservatism.

At the same time, soccer has never been as systematized as it is now; it's often how effectively managers resolve that contradiction that determines whether or not they are successful. The tension can produce positive results: it's a matter of taste more than anything else, but there were many who preferred the Barcelona side that won the Champions League under Luis Enrique in 2015 to the Guardiola model. Certainly, by having three soloists, in Messi, Luis Suárez, and Neymar, they had greater variety to their attack, more ways of breaking down a packed defense, even if the whole felt less pure, less of an expression of an ideal, than the team of four years earlier.

Soccer, by 2018, was in a distinctly post-Cruyffian age, and the influence of those who had played or coached at Barcelona in the late nineties was everywhere to be seen. But that style was never entirely dominant. Even when Guardiola's Bayern and Manchester City sides were dominant in their domestic leagues, they retained a vulnerability that ended up undoing them in the Champions League. In each of his three seasons in Germany, Guardiola won the championship with ease, breaking records and essentially ending the title race as a contest long before Christmas. In 2013-2014, Bayern conceded twenty-three goals in thirty-four games. The following season, they let in eighteen, then seventeen. It was a similar story in his second season in England, in 2017-2018, when City wrapped up the league with five games remaining, conceding roughly two-thirds of a goal per game. That suggests defensive stability, and yet in 2014 Bayern went out of the Champions League in the semifinal, losing 1-0 and 4-0 to Real Madrid, and in the 2015 semi they lost the first leg of their semifinal 3-0 to Barça as they suffered a 5-3 aggregate defeat. In 2018, City lost 3-0 and 2-1 to Klopp's Liverpool in the Champions League quarterfinal. They were defensively strong, in other words, apart from in certain games when they collapsed. His sides had a habit, in big games, of leaking three goals in twenty-minute spells: City had also let in three in quick succession in their 4-3 league defeat at Anfield in 2017-2018. Even in a league game against Leicester in 2016-2017, they'd gone 3-0 down in twenty minutes.

What was significant about the opponents wasn't just their quality but their style, or at least the style they adopted in the key moments of those games. Bypass the press, attack at pace, and Guardiola's sides were not just vulnerable but prone to panic. There's not only a psychological dimension-does the obsessive focus on the system perhaps deny players the individuality that would allow them, in difficult circumstances, to demonstrate the initiative to yank a game back their way? Do Guardiola's players, as Zlatan Ibrahimović claimed, become in some way little more than obedient schoolchildren?-but also a tactical one. It's no coincidence that the manager with by far the best record against Guardiola is Klopp, with eight wins in fourteen meetings. To say Klopp's high-tempo *Gegen-pressing* style is the best or only countermeasure to Guardiola's positional game is oversimplistic-City, after all, while losing three games out of four to Liverpool in 2017-2018, won the other one 5-0-but it does seem a way of taking it on that exposes its vulnerabilities.

It may be that this is always the way after an ideological revolution. Once the first blast of the new way's radicalism is over, what remains feels necessarily like a compromise. While there is a general sense of the pre-eminence of pressing, there is no side dragging football in a direction it feels like everyone else must follow. False nines are accepted and understood but far from common. The back three has returned to fashion but is not universal. Most but not all top sides play with a high line. Goalkeepers now are expected to be able to play with their feet, to be comfortable outside the box. The Real Madrid side that won three Champions Leagues in four years were obviously hugely talented, but they won't be remembered for any tactical innovation. This second decade of the twenty-first century feels like a period of retrenchment rather than radicalism. Nobody has been capable of playing in quite the same way as Guardiola's Barça, but equally nobody could ignore the lessons they had taught.

# [EPILOGUE](toc.xhtml#toc-epilogue)

I t would be easy to survey modern soccer and insist there can be nothing new. Roberto Mancini, in fact, did just that at a lecture he gave in Belgrade in 2007, arguing that future advances in soccer would come not in tactics but in the physical preparation of players. To an extent he is probably right. Soccer is a mature game that has been examined and analyzed relentlessly for almost a century and a half, and, assuming the number of players remains constant at eleven, there probably is no revolution waiting to astonish the world. Even if there is, even if some coach in some unlikely corner happens upon some radical departure, it will not have the stunning impact that, say, Hungary's withdrawn center-forward had in the early fifties. Even that was, as I hope this book has demonstrated, part of a continuum, drawing directly from Matthias Sindelar's interpretation of the center-forward's role in the Austrian *Wunderteam* , and having a parallel in Martim Francisco's work with Vila Nova.

England could not deal in 1931 with Sindelar dropping off, British sides struggled to cope with Vsevolod Bobrov doing the same when Dinamo Moscow toured in 1945, and they were humiliated by Nándor Hidegkuti in 1953. Lessons, evidently, should have been learned, but that they were not is explicable by the fact that those three examples were isolated and spread over twenty-two years. These days, Hungary's *Aranycsapat* would not have come to London as a mystery: their successes would have been seen on television, videos would have been picked over, and the movement of their players would have been analyzed by computer. A tactical innovation will never again spring up as a surprise.

Besides which, a talented Hungarian coach such as Gusztav Sebes would almost certainly not be working in Hungary, but would have followed the money to Western Europe. As cross-pollination between different soccer cultures increases, so national styles become less distinct. We are not yet homogenized, and probably never will be, but the trend is in that direction.

And yet there are always imaginations ready to defy expectation. For a long time, a promoted side, particularly one with limited resources, would usually adopt a defensive style. Spoil the game, the logic goes, restrict the influence of skill, reduce the number of goals likely to be scored, and a weaker team increases its chances of stealing a draw or a 1-0 win. Yet in 2006-2007, Pasquale Marino, having led Catania to promotion to Serie A the previous season, had his side play a 4-3-3 with attacking full-backs and no holding midfielder. They were encouraged not to play the percentages, but to try the outrageous and the difficult. Occasionally they came unstuck-they were hammered 7-0 by Roma, for instance-but exuberance proved just as hard to play against as dourness. Following the murder of a policeman during rioting at the derby against Palermo in February, Catania were banned from playing games at their home stadium, but they still finished as high as thirteenth. It wasn't a new system, but it was a revolution of style, a rebellion against convention. Since then the Premier League has seen the likes of Norwich City and Swansea City succeed while defying the stereotype.

Old styles can be successfully reintroduced in new contexts, particularly in the shortened form of major tournaments. Greece, for instance, at Euro 2004, were the only team who played without a zonal-marking back four. Their coach, Otto Rehhagel, employed a *libero* with three man-markers and then added further solidity with a five-man midfield and a lone striker. "Rehhagel won because he posed a problem people had forgotten how to solve," said Andy Roxburgh. "It wasn't fashionable but it was effective. They controlled matches without having control of the ball. Otto's view was: why should he try a watered-down version of somebody else's system? Whatever you say about his system, you have to admit that Greece got the ball into attack very quickly every time they had possession."

France, in particular, seemed to struggle against Greece, losing 1-0 to them in the quarterfinal. "They needed to get the ball to Thierry Henry faster," Roxburgh said. "Henry is at his most dangerous running into the centre from the left or running just left of centre. Against Greece, he drifted too wide because he wasn't getting any space. That's one of the things you want to do: push a threat to the touchline. Greece's opponents weren't used to being marked so tightly. The old method turned out to be a novelty."

When Spain won Euro 2012 playing often without a striker, it didn't come as a shock; it was seen merely as the progression of trends that had been traced over the previous few years. Barcelona's excellence, similarly, was revolutionary in degree rather than in conception; they simply did what others had done before but better and more so.

At the moment, use of strikerless formations is restricted to a tiny handful of elite clubs. Perhaps the 4-6-0 will, in time, become just as much the orthodoxy as 4-4-2 was in England until the midnineties, or the *libero* was in Italy until the late eighties; perhaps it will prove merely a passing fad. Certainly its emergence hints at the death of the old-fashioned striker in favor of something more versatile, and the move to universality, it can be said with some confidence, is an ongoing trend-even Robert Lewandowski, who resembles Ian Rush and has the physique an old fashioned target man, is comfortable pulling wide and dropping deep. Then again, perhaps that simply proves Mancini's point, and all that is actually happening is that the technicians of old are, thanks to improved nutrition and better training methods, becoming physically more imposing; if everybody is fit and powerful, then there is necessarily less demand for those players who offer little beyond their physique or their engine. If strikers are heading the way of old-school wingers and playmakers, though, then the question is who next? Center-backs, maybe? After all, if there is no center-forward to mark, the second center-back in a 4-4-2 would seem as redundant as the third in a 3-5-2 playing against a lone forward.

It is hard to believe, equally, that the increasingly detailed analysis afforded by technology will not also make a difference. Computers and a knowledge of cybernetics helped Valeriy Lobanovskyi devise his system, and it stands to reason that the more sophisticated technology becomes, the more sophisticated systems will become. The biggest obstacle to that, in fact, are the egos of players. Puffed up by years of immense wages and celebrity status, are they willing, as Lobanovskyi and Arrigo Sacchi demanded, to sacrifice themselves utterly to the collective? The experience of Real Madrid in the *galácticos* era suggests not.

That, perhaps, is the other side of the paradox at which Jorge Valdano hinted when he spoke of television's influence on the modern game: that it is the very popularity of soccer that prevents its advancement. Fans, arguably, are complicit in that. Terraces tend to conservatism, and the example of Sweden in the seventies indicates that there is a love of individualism-of soccer of first-order complexity, to use Tomas Petterson's term-that exceeds the demand for victory. Argentina's experiences as the period of *la nuestra* came to an end show just how damaging that decadence-of thought, if nothing else-can be. That said, globalization is a built-in defense; if nobody is progressing, then nobody is being left behind, so a wake-up like Argentina's 6-1 defeat to Czechoslovakia in 1958 is unlikely, unless a country outside the soccer mainstream is suddenly blessed with a hugely gifted generation of players who can resist the lures of Western European materialism long enough to submit themselves to the system of a tactically astute coach. South Korea's success in reaching the semifinal of the 2002 World Cup is evidence of what can be achieved with rigorous organization, even with essentially average players.

When he left Real Madrid, Sacchi said he found it "remarkable, worrying" that there had been no significant tactical development since the radical systematized approach of his Milan, but he remained convinced evolution would continue. "As long as humanity exists," he said, "something new will come along. Otherwise football dies." What came along was Barcelona. "Like my Milan," Sacchi said, "this team mark a 'before' and 'after' in world football."

The immediate time after was characterized by Bayern Munich and Borussia Dortmund, two teams who took the essential Van Gaal/Bielsa principles-from Van Gaal himself in Bayern's case-and sped them up. It is a truth-hinted at by Menotti's dictum that the point of training is to increase the speed at which a team can be precise-that seems written in the internal rhythms of soccer: each new form is developed and modified, made faster, until it reaches a maximum pace at which a new innovation arises to replace it. What Bayern Munich did was to take the Barcelona model and improve it, not so much with technical innovation as with physical.

What Barcelona had done with their phalanx of 5′7″ geniuses, Bayern did with players who were bigger, faster, and more direct. Bayern perhaps didn't hit quite the same levels of filigree passing as Barça at their peak, but they were not far off, and what was striking in that Champions League semifinal was how tired-how weak-Barcelona looked. Of course, it's not entirely fair to compare a team on the rise with one coming to the end of its cycle-one is hungry, desperately eager for success, and the other is sated, lacking the drive to suffer to stay in a game-but equally it can hardly be denied that Bayern's players were bigger than Barça's.

Guardiola's Barça felt like a pinnacle that would not be surpassed in a long time-if ever-and yet, within two years of their peak at Wembley, Bayern, on the stage, completed a Champions League victory that suggested that they were capable of even greater heights. They never quite scaled them, not even under Guardiola. His Manchester City, similarly, has seemed brilliant but flawed. It would take a peculiarly one-eyed view of the world not to acknowledge Guardiola's genius, and yet it increasingly seems that the Barcelona of 2011 may have been his finest side. After all, no matter how great a manager, he is still to an extent reliant on circumstance, and then he was working with an exceptional squad, the majority of whom had grown up at the club and been schooled in the Barça style.

And so what remains is not one hegemonic style, but a multiplicity of approaches, in part conditioned by Guardiola's Barça. And so, the wider soccer world joins Sacchi in awaiting the next great step. It may take time, but it will come. Many before have hailed the end of history; none have ever been right.

Jonathan Wilson's *Inverting the Pyramid* was football book of the year in the UK and Italy and was shortlisted for the William Hill Sports Book of the Year Award. His other books include *Behind the Curtain: Travels in Eastern European Football* ; *Sunderland: A Club Transformed* ; *The Anatomy of England: A History in Ten Matches* ; *Nobody Ever Says Thank You* , a critically acclaimed biography of Brian Clough; *The Outsider: A History of the Goalkeeper* ; *Angels With Dirty Faces: How Argentinian Soccer Defined a Nation and Changed the Game Forever* ; *The Anatomy of Liverpool* and *The Anatomy of Manchester United* . He also writes for the *Guardian* , *Sports Illustrated* , and *World Soccer* , and he is the editor of *The Blizzard* .
